description: Somos estudiantes de la Universidad Catolica Argentina (UCA), de la carrera Lic en Ciencia de Datos.
summary:
We developed an interface for the first astronauts walking on Mars. It turns NASA mission data into one astronaut-centred, heading-up radar that intends to answer these three questions: Where can I walk? How much time do I have? What is next?

We answer them by joining NASA data from Gale Crater. Slopes with an inclination higher than 20° appear in red, and a green modelled route leads through six science stops (Where can I walk?). An EVA clock, the return margin and an amber line show how far the crew can go and still reach the rover in time (How much time do I have?). Each stop , clicking on it, shows its distance, arrival time and the real photo Curiosity took there (What is next?).

Everything is visible at a glance in three views: the radar, centred on the astronaut; an overview of the whole route; and a first-person 3D view through the helmet visor, with spoken alerts when a limit is crossed.
details:
What it does and how it works

Marswalk Radar has two halves. An offline Python pipeline downloads NASA data, processes it, and writes a small static data package. A browser viewer built with three.js reads only that package: no backend, no external requests.

The pipeline works in four steps:

It computes slope from a 2 m HiRISE elevation model of Gale Crater and marks every cell steeper than 20° as a hazard.

It builds a walking graph of almost one million 4 m cells, where the cost of each step is walking time from a hiking-speed curve. Steep cells are blocked, and paths are not allowed to cut corners between blocked cells.

It finds the modelled route through six science stops with Dijkstra’s algorithm.

It computes the walking time from every cell back to the pickup rover.

The default scenario is two astronauts walking from Pahrump Hills to Hematite Hotspot. The route is 5.34 km: 4 h 43 min of a 6 h EVA budget, with a steepest slope of 19.1° and a minimum return margin of 77 min. It never touches a blocked cell, and 57 % of it lies within 50 m of Curiosity’s real track.

The viewer has three views that share one mission clock:

Radar: the crew at the centre, heading up.

Overview: the whole area, north up.

3D: first person through a helmet visor.

Cards show the slope underfoot, the steepest slope ahead, time remaining and the return margin. An amber line marks how far the crew can go and still reach the rover in time. It follows the terrain instead of being a circle, and it shrinks as the clock runs. Each stop opens Curiosity’s Navcam photos taken at that spot, with distance, arrival time and elevation change. A scout robot drives the route 90 min ahead of the crew. In 3D, a RADIATION card shows what Curiosity’s RAD measured over 2012–2026 for that day and hour. A simulation panel lets you set oxygen, CO₂, suit pressure, atmospheric pressure, radiation and time of day. When a value crosses its limit, the tablet plays a chime and speaks an alert.

Benefits and intended impact

The radar replaces scattered archives with three glanceable answers. That lowers the crew’s mental load and supports their decisions when Earth is up to 22 minutes away by radio. Because the scenario lives in one configuration file, the same pipeline can generate a map for another landing site.

Tools

Python: NumPy, SciPy (ndimage, sparse.csgraph), pandas, tifffile, Pillow, PyYAML, Requests, pytest.

JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS, with no framework and no build step.

three.js r187 with custom GLSL shaders.

Web Audio API and Web Speech API, both on-device.

Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages.

Creativity

A first-person radar instead of a static map.

A return limit derived from the terrain.

A scout robot ahead of the crew.

A helmet-visor view with spoken alerts.

Curiosity’s own photos as a preview of each stop.

Factors we considered

Safety: a hard slope limit, the return margin, radiation and suit conditions.

Data resolution: we dropped layers too coarse for a walk, such as THEMIS (81 m/px) and the global geologic map. We also tested HiRISE brightness as a sand detector and rejected it, because it did not separate sand from rock.

Scientific honesty: everything is labelled simulated or historical; there is no mSv conversion; assumptions are visible in the interface.

Offline operation: there is no internet on Mars, so the viewer makes no external requests.

Reproducibility: every file is logged with its URL and SHA-256 checksum, the package rebuilds with one command, and the pipeline has tests.
